output.title: Traceability starts with one workflow, not everything
output.body:
Rethinking traceability is not about making every process visible. For a small business, it usually means choosing one recurring workflow where you keep asking the same question: who did what, when, and why, and can I prove it fast enough to make a decision?

A good place to start is the work that forces repeated manual checking. That might be invoice-to-payment matching, a customer-question-to-resolution log, or a refund dispute where the paper trail is scattered across email, spreadsheets, and a payment tool. If the answer takes too long to reconstruct, traceability is already part of the cost of doing business.

The practical decision is simple: compare the time you spend tracing the record by hand with the risk of automating the wrong step. If the workflow is frequent, repetitive, and leaves an audit trail that matters later, it may be worth automating the trace. If it depends on judgment, exceptions, or payment approval, keep the human in the loop.

That boundary matters. Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Automation can collect and organise the trail; it should not quietly take over the final call.

If you want a quick self-check, ask this: could you show the full chain of events for one recent case today without rebuilding the story from scratch? If not, traceability is worth examining before you add more manual work.
